newsitem.title: NEPAL: Communists gain ground in Nepal by-elections.
newsitem.headline: Communists gain ground in Nepal by-elections.

text.p: Nepal's opposition communists have strengthened their hand in parliament with three by-election victories and compounded troubles for Prime Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba's coalition, analysts said on Tuesday.
The Unified Marxist-Leninist (UML) party won three of five by-elections held last week, according to final results announced late on Monday.
The communists, the biggest party in the 205-member lower house of parliament, increased their strength to 90 deputies from 87.
Deuba's centrist Nepali Congress party, which leads a fractious three-party coalition, raised its representation to 87 from 85 by winning the two other by-elections.
The by-elections were the first popular vote since Deuba took power in the Himalayan kingdom in September 1995.
Deuba narrowly survived a no-confidence motion in December when the communist-led opposition fell two votes short of toppling their rivals.
"The problem of (Deuba's) instability remains intact," said Badri Bahadur Karki, a constitutional lawyer in the capital Kathmandu.

The by-elections were considered a setback for Deuba, who saw the communist UML regain two constituencies it had held before and take a third from the Rastriya Prajatantra Party (RPP), a partner in the ruling coalition.
Voters returned Nepali Congress candidates in the two constituencies where Deuba's party won.
"The outcome is the reflection of the organisational weaknesses and non-performance of the government," said Nepali Congress general secretary Shushil Koirala.
"People have rejected Deuba and UML should stake its claim to form a minority government," said UML central committee member Pradeep Nepal.
Deuba, who replaced a communist government in 1995, has limped from crisis to crisis and struggled to keep his minority coalition together.
Nepali Congress is backed by the RPP, which has 19 deputies, and the Nepal Sudbhavana Party (NSP), which has two.
December's no-confidence vote was triggered when seven government ministers from the RPP defected from the cabinet.

The lower house rejected the communist-backed no-confidence motion by 101 votes to 84, two short of a 103-vote majority. The five seats which were filled in last week's by-elections were vacant at the time of the no-confidence vote.

Earlier this month five of the seven RPP rebels who had defected rallied to the side of Deuba, who has vowed to seek a vote of confidence in the next session of parliament scheduled to begin in late Fabruary.
While Deuba commands a majority on paper, a festering split in the RPP's ranks has raised doubts about the prime minister's ability to win a confidence motion.
Parliamentary elections are not scheduled until 1999 in the kingdom, which ushered in multi-party rule in 1990 under a constitutional monarchy after a bloody pro-democracy movement.
